section: What you are setting up, in plain words
text:
What you are setting up, in plain words

R is the programming language.
RStudio is the program you write R in. It also includes Quarto, the tool that turns your .qmd pages into a website.
Git is a program on your computer that records the history of your files (each saved snapshot is a commit).
GitHub is a website that stores a copy of that history online (your repository, or repo). Sending your commits there is called a push.
Netlify is a website host. It watches your GitHub repository and publishes your rendered site every time you push.

The chain is: edit in RStudio, render with Quarto, commit and push with Git, and Netlify publishes. Nothing is published that you did not push.

Step 1: Install R

Go to https://cran.r-project.org
Windows: click “Download R for Windows”, then “base”, then the download link. Run the installer with the defaults.
Mac: click “Download R for macOS”. Pick arm64 if your Mac has an Apple chip (M1 to M4) or x86_64 for an older Intel Mac (Apple menu, About This Mac, tells you). Run the installer.

Step 2: Install RStudio Desktop

Go to https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/ and download RStudio Desktop (free) for your system. Install with the defaults.
Open RStudio. In the Console type 1 + 1 and press Enter. If you see [1] 2, R and RStudio are talking to each other.
Quarto is included in RStudio; you do not install it separately.

section: Step 3: Install the R packages the course uses
text:
Step 3: Install the R packages the course uses
In the Console, run this line and wait for it to finish (it can take several minutes the first time):
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "usethis", "gitcreds", "rmarkdown"))
Check it worked:
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
Both should load with no error (messages listing packages are fine).

Step 4: Install Git
Git is separate from GitHub and must be installed on your computer.

Windows: go to https://git-scm.com/download/win, download “Git for Windows”, install with the defaults.
Mac: open the Terminal app (Applications, Utilities, Terminal), type git --version and press Enter. If Git is missing, macOS offers to install the command line tools; accept and wait.
Restart RStudio after installing Git. Then in the Console:

usethis::use_git_config(user.name = "Your Name", user.email = "you@students.niu.edu")
Use the same email you will use for GitHub in the next step.

Step 5: Create your GitHub account

Go to https://github.com and sign up with your university email.
Pick a username you would be comfortable putting on a resume: this repository is part of your portfolio.
Optional but worth it: apply for the GitHub Student Developer Pack at https://education.github.com/pack (free tools with a student email).

section: Step 6: Create your project repository from the template
text:
Step 6: Create your project repository from the template

Open the class template: https://github.com/biagiopalese/681_rstudio_template (the same link is posted in the Dr. B Learning Arena).
Click Use this template, then Create a new repository. This makes an independent copy under your own account (it is not a fork, so there is no link back to the class template).
Name it something a recruiter can read (for example qsr-demand-analysis), choose Private, click Create repository. Private means only you and the collaborators you invite (Step 9) can see it. After grades are posted you may switch it to Public to show it as a portfolio piece (Settings, General, Danger Zone, Change visibility).
On your new repository page click the green Code button and copy the HTTPS address (it ends in .git). You need it in Step 7.

If the template was given to you as a zip instead: unzip it, then in Step 7 use File, New Project, Existing Directory, pick the folder, and afterwards run usethis::use_github() in the Console to create the GitHub repository from it.

section: Step 7: Open the repository in RStudio
text:
Step 7: Open the repository in RStudio

In RStudio: File, New Project, Version Control, Git.
Paste the HTTPS address from Step 6 into “Repository URL”. Choose where on your computer the folder should live. Click Create Project.
RStudio downloads (clones) the repository and opens it as a Project. From now on, always open your work by double-clicking the .Rproj file in that folder, or through File, Open Project.

section: Step 8: Connect RStudio to GitHub with a personal access token
text:
Step 8: Connect RStudio to GitHub with a personal access token
GitHub does not accept your account password from RStudio. It accepts a personal access token (PAT), a long code that acts as a password for tools.

In the Console run:

usethis::create_github_token()
A browser page opens on GitHub with the right settings pre-selected. In the “Note” field write something like OMIS 681 laptop. Leave the expiration and the pre-checked boxes as they are, scroll down, click Generate token. 2. Copy the token shown (it starts with ghp_). You will never see it again, so copy it now. 3. Back in the Console run:
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()
When asked for the password or token, paste the token and press Enter. 4. Confirm everything is connected:
usethis::git_sitrep()
Look for your name, your email, and “Personal access token: ”. If it says , repeat this step.
Tokens expire (the default is 30 days). When RStudio starts asking for a password again, create a new token with the same two commands.

section: Step 9: Add Dr. B as a collaborator (required for grading)
text:
Step 9: Add Dr. B as a collaborator (required for grading)

On your repository page on GitHub: Settings, then Collaborators (left menu), then Add people.
Enter biagiopalese and click Add biagiopalese to this repository.
Dr. B receives an invitation by email and accepts it. Until then the Collaborators page shows the invitation as pending, which is fine for your screenshot.

Because the repository is private, this step is the only way Dr. B can see your work. Skipping it means your milestones cannot be graded.

section: Step 10: Render your site for the first time
text:
Step 10: Render your site for the first time

In RStudio with your Project open, find the Build pane (top right; if you do not see it, click Build in the menu bar) and click Render Website.
RStudio creates a folder called _site containing the finished web pages and shows the home page in the Viewer.
If Render stops with “there is no package called …”, install that package (Step 3 pattern) and render again.
In the template, the code chunks that load packages start switched off (eval: false). Once Step 3 is done, change false to true in those chunks so your code runs.

Step 11: Commit and push

Click the Git tab (top right pane). Every changed file is listed.
Tick the Staged box next to each file (including the _site folder: Netlify publishes exactly what is in there).
Click Commit, write one short sentence describing the change (for example “first render of the site”), click Commit, close the window.
Click Push (green arrow). If a login appears, paste your token (Step 8).
Refresh your repository page on GitHub: your files are there.

The data folder and any .csv file never appear in the Git tab: the template’s .gitignore file keeps them out on purpose. Leave that as it is.

section: Step 12: Create your Netlify site from the repository
text:
Step 12: Create your Netlify site from the repository

Go to https://app.netlify.com and choose Sign up with GitHub. This links the two accounts in one step.
Click Add new project, then Import an existing project, then GitHub. Authorize Netlify when asked and pick your repository. A private repository works here: Netlify asks for permission to read your repositories, and you can limit it to this one. Your site is public even though the repository is private, which is exactly what you want.
In the settings screen: leave Build command empty, set Publish directory to _site. Click Deploy.
Netlify gives your site a random name. Change it under Project configuration (also called Site configuration), General, Site details, Change site name.
Open the address Netlify shows. Your site is live.

Because the site is imported from GitHub, every push republishes it automatically. If you ever see “Page not found” after a push, the usual reason is that _site was not committed: render, stage _site, commit, push.

Step 13: The rhythm from here
Every working session: open the .Rproj, edit, Render Website, Commit, Push. Small pushes often beat one giant push before a deadline, and the commit history is part of how your work is graded.

section: Step 14: Screenshots for the Software Pre-Flight ticket
text:
Step 14: Screenshots for the Software Pre-Flight ticket

RStudio with a successfully rendered page in the Viewer.
Your GitHub profile page.
Your repository’s Collaborators page showing Dr. B added.
Your live Netlify site in a browser, address visible.

Troubleshooting

“there is no package called X”: run install.packages("X") and try again.
RStudio keeps asking for a GitHub password: your token expired or was not stored. Repeat Step 8.
Push rejected: someone (usually you, on another computer) pushed changes your copy does not have. Click Pull first, then Push.
Render fails at a code chunk: read the first line of the error; it names the chunk and the problem. Fix that chunk; do not delete it.
Netlify shows an old version: check that the last commit reached GitHub (refresh the repository page) and that _site is in that commit.
Everything is broken and you do not know why: post in the Dr. B Learning Arena with the exact error text. Screenshots of red text help.

title: Exploration
Exploration
text:
Marketplace benchmark
Before comparing seller groups, I first calculated overall marketplace performance.


Code
overall_performance <- supply_chain_data |>
  summarise(
    total_items = n(),
    average_delivery_days = mean(delivery_days),
    average_freight_cost = mean(freight_value),
    average_freight_ratio = mean(freight_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    on_time_rate = mean(delivery_status == "On Time") * 100
  )

overall_performance


# A tibble: 1 × 5
  total_items average_delivery_days average_freight_cost average_freight_ratio
        <int>                 <dbl>                <dbl>                 <dbl>
1      110189                  12.0                 20.0                 0.321
# ℹ 1 more variable: on_time_rate <dbl>


The marketplace contains 110189 item rows.
Average delivery time is 12 days, average freight cost is 20, and the overall on-time delivery rate is 92.6%.
These values provide the benchmark for the rest of the analysis.


Code
state_names <- tibble(
  seller_state = c(
    "SP", "MG", "PR", "RJ",
    "SC", "RS", "DF", "BA"
  ),
  seller_name = c(
    "São Paulo",
    "Minas Gerais",
    "Paraná",
    "Rio de Janeiro",
    "Santa Catarina",
    "Rio Grande do Sul",
    "Federal District",
    "Bahia"
  )
)

seller_state_performance <- supply_chain_data |>
  group_by(seller_state) |>
  summarise(
    total_items = n(),
    average_delivery_days = mean(delivery_days),
    average_freight_cost = mean(freight_value),
    average_freight_ratio = mean(freight_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    on_time_rate = mean(delivery_status == "On Time") * 100,
    average_product_weight = mean(product_weight_g, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_items)) |>
  left_join(state_names, by = "seller_state")

top_8_states <- seller_state_performance |>
  head(8)

largest_state <- top_8_states |>
  arrange(desc(total_items)) |>
  head(1)

largest_state_share <-
  largest_state$total_items /
  overall_performance$total_items * 100

title: Exploration
text:
1. Where scale meets reliability
The first question is whether the seller groups handling the most marketplace activity are also delivering reliably.

1a. Volume and delivery performance
This chart combines marketplace volume, on-time delivery performance, and average freight cost.


Code
ggplot(
  top_8_states,
  aes(
    x = total_items,
    y = on_time_rate,
    size = average_freight_cost,
    color = seller_name
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = overall_performance$on_time_rate,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "#555555"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Scale does not always guarantee stronger fulfillment",
    subtitle = "Bubble size represents average freight cost",
    x = "Number of Items",
    y = "On-Time Delivery Rate (%)",
    color = "Seller State",
    size = "Average Freight Cost"
  ) +
  theme_light()









What this shows: São Paulo handles 78598 items, representing about 71.3% of marketplace activity.
Because of its scale, even a relatively small operational change in this seller group could affect a large number of marketplace items.


1b. Above or below the benchmark
The next chart compares each major seller state’s on-time delivery performance directly with the marketplace average.


Code
delivery_comparison <- top_8_states |>
  mutate(
    difference_from_average =
      on_time_rate - overall_performance$on_time_rate
  )

best_delivery_state <- delivery_comparison |>
  arrange(desc(difference_from_average)) |>
  head(1)

weakest_delivery_state <- delivery_comparison |>
  arrange(difference_from_average) |>
  head(1)




Code
ggplot(
  delivery_comparison,
  aes(
    x = difference_from_average,
    y = reorder(seller_name, difference_from_average)
  )
) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "#555555"
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(
      x = 0,
      xend = difference_from_average,
      y = reorder(seller_name, difference_from_average),
      yend = reorder(seller_name, difference_from_average)
    ),
    linewidth = 1,
    color = "#6C757D"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(color = difference_from_average > 0),
    size = 4
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "TRUE" = "#2A9D8F",
      "FALSE" = "#E63946"
    ),
    labels = c(
      "FALSE" = "Below Average",
      "TRUE" = "Above Average"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Major seller states fall on both sides of the delivery benchmark",
    subtitle = "Distance from the overall marketplace on-time rate",
    x = "Percentage Points Above or Below Marketplace Average",
    y = "Seller State",
    color = "Performance"
  ) +
  theme_light()









What this shows: Rio Grande do Sul performs strongest relative to the marketplace benchmark, while São Paulo has the weakest performance among the eight largest seller states.
This matters because weak performance becomes more important when it occurs in a seller group handling substantial marketplace volume.

title: Exploration
text:
2. Where operations start to slip
Delivery performance and freight burden should not be evaluated separately.
A seller group with strong delivery and low freight burden occupies a very different operating position from one with weaker delivery and higher freight cost relative to product price.


Code
ggplot(
  top_8_states,
  aes(
    x = average_freight_ratio,
    y = on_time_rate,
    size = total_items,
    color = seller_name
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = overall_performance$average_freight_ratio,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "#555555"
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = overall_performance$on_time_rate,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "#555555"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Seller states occupy very different operating positions",
    subtitle = "Bubble size represents marketplace item volume",
    x = "Average Freight-to-Price Ratio",
    y = "On-Time Delivery Rate (%)",
    color = "Seller State",
    size = "Number of Items"
  ) +
  theme_light()









What this shows: Seller groups above the horizontal benchmark have stronger-than-average delivery performance.
Seller groups to the right of the vertical benchmark have a higher-than-average freight burden.
The groups that combine weaker delivery with higher freight burden deserve the closest operational attention, especially when their bubbles are large.

title: Exploration
text:
3. When does marketplace pressure peak?
Seller performance should also be viewed through time.
A seller network may operate differently during low-volume and high-volume periods, so I summarized marketplace activity by month and year.


Code
monthly_activity <- supply_chain_data |>
  group_by(purchase_year, purchase_month) |>
  summarise(
    total_items = n(),
    on_time_rate = mean(delivery_status == "On Time") * 100
  )


`summarise()` has regrouped the output.
ℹ Summaries were computed grouped by purchase_year and purchase_month.
ℹ Output is grouped by purchase_year.
ℹ Use `summarise(.groups = "drop_last")` to silence this message.
ℹ Use `summarise(.by = c(purchase_year, purchase_month))` for per-operation
  grouping (`?dplyr::dplyr_by`) instead.


Code
peak_month <- monthly_activity |>
  arrange(desc(total_items)) |>
  head(1)



Area + line + points
The area emphasizes the amount of marketplace activity.
The line shows the direction of change, while the points make individual months easier to identify.


Code
ggplot(
  monthly_activity,
  aes(
    x = purchase_month,
    y = total_items,
    group = 1
  )
) +
  geom_area(
    fill = "#4CC9F0",
    alpha = 0.45
  ) +
  geom_line(
    color = "#3A0CA3",
    linewidth = 1.3
  ) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#F72585",
    size = 3
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ purchase_year) +
  labs(
    title = "Marketplace pressure changes sharply across the year",
    subtitle = "Area shows volume while the line and points highlight the monthly pattern",
    x = "Purchase Month",
    y = "Number of Items"
  ) +
  theme_light()









What this shows: The highest-volume period occurs in month 11 of 2017, with 8474 items.
The on-time delivery rate during that period was approximately 87.1%.
This helps management identify when the marketplace is experiencing its greatest fulfillment workload.

title: Exploration
text:
4. Cost or product mix?
Higher freight cost does not automatically mean that a seller is operating inefficiently.
Product characteristics may explain part of the freight burden.

4a. Does weight explain freight cost?


Code
supply_chain_data |>
  filter(!is.na(product_weight_g)) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = product_weight_g,
      y = freight_value
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#4361EE",
    alpha = 0.12
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    color = "#F72585",
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1.4
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Heavier products generally cost more to ship",
    subtitle = "The highlighted trend shows the overall relationship",
    x = "Product Weight (grams)",
    y = "Freight Cost"
  ) +
  theme_light()









What this shows: Freight cost generally rises as product weight increases.
This means higher freight cost should not automatically be treated as evidence of weak seller performance.
Product mix explains at least part of the logistics difference.


4b. Does the pattern change by seller state?
The next chart takes the overall relationship from 4.a and separates it across the four largest seller states.
The observations are kept light so the state-specific trend lines become the main focus.


Code
top_4_states <- top_8_states |>
  head(4)

top_4_state_names <- top_4_states$seller_name




Code
supply_chain_data |>
  left_join(state_names, by = "seller_state") |>
  filter(seller_name %in% top_4_state_names) |>
  filter(!is.na(product_weight_g)) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = product_weight_g,
      y = freight_value
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(
    color = "gray60",
    alpha = 0.12
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    aes(color = seller_name),
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1.4
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ seller_name) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "São Paulo" = "#F72585",
      "Minas Gerais" = "#4361EE",
      "Paraná" = "#F8961E",
      "Rio de Janeiro" = "#2A9D8F"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Product weight matters, but the freight pattern changes by state",
    subtitle = "Each colored trend highlights the weight–freight relationship within a major seller state",
    x = "Product Weight (grams)",
    y = "Freight Cost",
    color = "Seller State"
  ) +
  guides(
    color = "none"
  ) +
  theme_light()









What this shows: All four major seller states show a positive relationship between product weight and freight cost, but the strength and shape of that relationship are not identical.
The colored lines make these differences easier to compare.
This suggests that product weight explains part of the freight burden, while seller location and other fulfillment factors may still contribute.

title: Exploration
text:
5. Are averages hiding risk?
Average freight cost can hide important differences in the underlying shipment distribution.
For this reason, the next chart combines two geoms:

violin plot → shows the overall distribution,
boxplot → highlights the center and spread.



Code
top_5_states <- top_8_states |>
  head(5)

top_5_state_names <- top_5_states$seller_name

highest_freight_state <- top_5_states |>
  arrange(desc(average_freight_cost)) |>
  head(1)




Code
supply_chain_data |>
  left_join(state_names, by = "seller_state") |>
  filter(seller_name %in% top_5_state_names) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = seller_name,
      y = freight_value,
      fill = seller_name,
      color = seller_name
    )
  ) +
  geom_violin(
    alpha = 0.45
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.14,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "São Paulo" = "#F72585",
      "Minas Gerais" = "#4361EE",
      "Paraná" = "#F8961E",
      "Rio de Janeiro" = "#2A9D8F",
      "Santa Catarina" = "#9B5DE5"
    )
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "São Paulo" = "#F72585",
      "Minas Gerais" = "#4361EE",
      "Paraná" = "#F8961E",
      "Rio de Janeiro" = "#2A9D8F",
      "Santa Catarina" = "#9B5DE5"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average freight cost hides very different shipment patterns",
    subtitle = "Violin shows the distribution while the boxplot highlights center and spread",
    x = "Seller State",
    y = "Freight Cost",
    fill = "Seller State",
    color = "Seller State"
  ) +
  guides(
    fill = "none",
    color = "none"
  ) +
  theme_light()









What this shows: Santa Catarina has the highest average freight cost among the five largest seller states, at approximately 26.
The distribution shows something that averages cannot.
Some seller states have a much wider freight-cost spread, meaning management may be dealing with occasional very expensive shipments rather than consistently high cost across every order.

title: Exploration
text:
6. What should management do next?
The exploration shows that seller performance should not be judged using volume, delivery performance, or freight cost alone.
The strongest seller groups are those that combine meaningful marketplace scale with reliable delivery and a reasonable freight burden.
Management should pay particular attention to seller groups that combine:

high marketplace volume,
delivery performance below the marketplace benchmark,
freight burden above the marketplace benchmark,
unusually wide freight-cost variation, and
freight costs that cannot be fully explained by heavier products.

The time analysis also identifies when marketplace workload reaches its highest levels.
Together, these findings help separate scalable seller performance from areas where targeted operational improvement could have the largest marketplace impact.

title: Scaling Smarter: Evaluating Seller Performance in an E-Commerce Marketplace
text:
Business scenario
An e-commerce marketplace depends on thousands of independent sellers to fulfill customer orders.
As the marketplace grows, management needs to understand whether the seller groups handling the most activity are also operating efficiently.
A seller group may handle a large number of items, but high delivery delays or high freight costs could make that growth harder to sustain.
This project looks at seller performance using marketplace volume, delivery reliability, freight cost, seller location, and product characteristics.

title: Scaling Smarter: Evaluating Seller Performance in an E-Commerce Marketplace
text:
Why this matters
The goal is to identify seller groups that support efficient marketplace growth and seller groups that may need closer attention.
The analysis also helps separate two different situations:

higher logistics costs caused by weaker operational performance, and
higher logistics costs that may be explained by the types of products being shipped.

This distinction is important because a seller should not automatically be considered inefficient just because it ships heavier or more expensive-to-transport products.

title: Scaling Smarter: Evaluating Seller Performance in an E-Commerce Marketplace
text:
How the analysis is organized
The project is structured in four stages:

Data — clean and combine the order, order-item, seller, and product datasets.
Exploration — compare seller groups using marketplace volume, delivery performance, and freight efficiency.
Modeling — build on the exploratory findings using the modeling methods introduced later in the course.
Conclusions — summarize the findings and connect them back to the business question.

title: Scaling Smarter: Evaluating Seller Performance in an E-Commerce Marketplace
text:
About this project
I am a graduate student interested in supply chain and business analytics.
This project uses R, ggplot2, and Quarto to analyze e-commerce fulfillment performance and turn the results into business recommendations.

title: Data

Data structure
I reviewed the structure of each dataset to understand the available variables and their data types.

Orders


Code
glimpse(orders)

title: Data
text:
Missing values
Before deciding how to clean the data, I checked how many missing values appear in each dataset.


Code
missing_summary <- tibble(
  dataset = c(
    "Orders",
    "Order Items",
    "Products",
    "Sellers"
  ),
  missing_values = c(
    sum(is.na(orders)),
    sum(is.na(order_items)),
    sum(is.na(products)),
    sum(is.na(sellers))
  )
)

missing_summary


# A tibble: 4 × 2
  dataset     missing_values
  <chr>                <int>
1 Orders                5930
2 Order Items              0
3 Products              2448
4 Sellers                  0


The orders and products datasets contain missing values, so I looked more closely at which variables are affected.

Missing values in orders


Code
orders_missing <- tibble(
  variable = names(orders),
  missing_values = colSums(is.na(orders))
) |>
  filter(missing_values > 0)

orders_missing


# A tibble: 2 × 2
  variable                      missing_values
  <chr>                                  <dbl>
1 order_delivered_customer_date           2965
2 delivery_days                           2965


The missing order values mainly affect delivery information.
Because this project evaluates fulfillment performance, orders without a usable delivery duration cannot be included in the delivery analysis.


Missing values in products

  variable = names(products),
  missing_values = colSums(is.na(products))
) |>
  filter(missing_values > 0)

These records are retained because those variables are not required for every part of the analysis. Missing product weight is removed only when a chart specifically uses product weight.

title: Data
text:
Cleaning the order data
The analysis focuses on completed deliveries.
I therefore kept only orders with a delivered status and a non-missing delivery duration.


Code
orders_clean <- orders |>
  filter(order_status == "delivered") |>
  filter(!is.na(delivery_days))


The effect of this cleaning step is shown below.


Code
order_cleaning_summary <- tibble(
  stage = c(
    "Original Orders",
    "Cleaned Delivered Orders"
  ),
  rows = c(
    nrow(orders),
    nrow(orders_clean)
  ),
  columns = c(
    ncol(orders),
    ncol(orders_clean)
  )
)

order_cleaning_summary


# A tibble: 2 × 3
  stage                     rows columns
  <chr>                    <int>   <int>
1 Original Orders          99441      11
2 Cleaned Delivered Orders 96470      11


A delivery-status variable is then created by comparing the actual delivery duration with the estimated delivery duration.


Code
orders_clean <- orders_clean |>
  mutate(
    delivery_status = if_else(
      delivery_days <= estimated_days,
      "On Time",
      "Late"
    )
  )




Code
delivery_status_summary <- orders_clean |>
  count(delivery_status) |>
  mutate(
    percent = n / sum(n) * 100
  )

delivery_status_summary


# A tibble: 2 × 3
  delivery_status     n percent
  <chr>           <int>   <dbl>
1 Late             7307    7.57
2 On Time         89163   92.4 


This gives the analysis a consistent way to compare delivery reliability across seller groups.

title: Data
text:
Creating the freight-to-price ratio
Freight cost alone does not show how large the shipping cost is relative to the value of the product.
For example, a freight charge of 20 has a much larger impact on a product priced at 40 than on a product priced at 400.
I therefore created a freight-to-price ratio.


Code
supply_chain_data <- supply_chain_data |>
  mutate(
    freight_ratio = freight_value / price
  )




Code
freight_ratio_summary <- supply_chain_data |>
  summarise(
    minimum = min(freight_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    average = mean(freight_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(freight_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    maximum = max(freight_ratio, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

freight_ratio_summary


# A tibble: 1 × 4
  minimum average median maximum
    <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>
1       0   0.321  0.232    26.2


The large difference between the median and maximum also shows that some products have unusually high freight costs relative to their price.
Rather than automatically removing those observations, I keep them because they may represent real costly shipments that are useful for the business analysis.

title: Data
text:
Variables used in the exploration
The main variables used in the Exploration page are:

seller_state — seller location
delivery_days — actual delivery duration
estimated_days — estimated delivery duration
delivery_status — on-time or late delivery
price — product selling price
freight_value — freight cost
freight_ratio — freight cost relative to product price
product_weight_g — product weight
seller_id — seller identifier
order_id — order identifier
